name: Garravogue

attributes.attribute: descends from the goddess the Cailleach
named for a witch who drowned in it
turned into a serpent by breaking the Sabbath

sources: Gwynn, Edward. The Metrical Dindshenchas. Part II. Vol. IX. Royal Irish Academy, Todd Lecture Series. Dublin: Hodges, Figgis, and Co., Ltd., 1906, 18.
MacNeill, Máire. The Festival of Lughnasa, Parts I and II. Dublin: Comhairle Bhéaloideas Éireann, 1982. Pp. 400-401, 517-522.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Garravogue is an Irish folkloric figure. Other names are Carravogue, Garbhóg, Ghearagáin, Garragh-Maw, and Garrawog. Two similar hag-like beings appear in Irish oral folklore. Both may descend from the ancient goddess called the Cailleach. The River Garravogue in County Sligo took its name from a witch. She fell into the water and drowned. The maiden Gile formed Lough Gill in the same way. The two may be one figure in maiden and hag form. Another tale is told in County Meath and County Cavan. In that tale Garrawog broke the Sabbath. She ate blackberries on her way to church. She became a giant serpent or a cannibal. Saint Patrick threw holy water at her. She then dissolved. In other versions his staff split her into four pieces.

okr.objective: Describe Garravogue as a hag-like Irish folkloric figure tied to the Cailleach.
key_results: The River Garravogue was named for a witch who drowned.
Garravogue may descend from the goddess the Cailleach.
Saint Patrick turned her serpent form to water or split her into four.
The story of Gile mirrors hers at Lough Gill.
